faqs.answer: 64 grams. USDA sizes are minimum weights per dozen: extra-large is 27 ounces per dozen, which works out to 2.25 ounces or 64 grams per egg. Individual eggs vary a little around that.

parts.meaning: The constant from the egg's thermal properties: density 1.038 g per cubic cm, specific heat 3.7, thermal conductivity 0.0054.
The weight of the egg in grams. An extra-large egg is 64 g (USDA size).
The starting temperature of the egg: 4°C from the fridge, 20°C at room temperature.
The boiling point of the water: 100°C at sea level, lower at altitude.
The target temperature at the edge of the yolk: 84°C for hard-boiled.
The yolk edge factor. The yolk is about a third of the egg, so its edge sits about 69 percent of the way from the center to the shell.

formula.text: Time = 27 × M^(2/3) × ln(0.76 × (Tegg - Twater) / (Tyolk - Twater)). For an extra-large fridge egg at sea level, hard-boiled: 27 × 64^(2/3) × ln(0.76 × (4 - 100) / (84 - 100)) = 657 seconds, about 10 minutes 55 seconds.

howToSteps.name: Boil the water first
howToSteps.text: Bring a saucepan of water to a full rolling boil. The formula assumes the egg goes into water that is already boiling.

howToSteps.name: Lower the eggs in
howToSteps.text: Lower each egg in gently on a spoon and start the timer at once. Keep the water at a gentle boil.

howToSteps.name: Time it
howToSteps.text: Boil an extra-large fridge egg for 10 minutes 55 seconds for hard-boiled. Soft is 4 minutes 55 seconds, jammy 5 minutes 55 seconds, and medium 6 minutes 25 seconds.

howToSteps.name: Ice bath
howToSteps.text: Move the eggs straight to ice water for 10 minutes. This stops the cooking and makes peeling easier.

howToSteps.name: Peel
howToSteps.text: Tap both ends on the counter, roll gently, and peel under cold running water.

title: How Long to Boil Extra-Large Eggs
tutorial: An extra-large egg weighs 64 grams against a large egg's 57, and those 7 grams add 25 seconds for a soft egg and 45 seconds for a hard one. Hard-boiled goes from 10 minutes 10 seconds to 10 minutes 55 seconds; soft goes from 4 minutes 30 seconds to 4 minutes 55 seconds. If you boil extra-large eggs on large-egg times, the yolk comes out a step softer than you asked for.

The time grows with the weight to the power of two thirds, which is why 7 grams does not add much. Doubling the weight would multiply the time by about 1.6, not 2. The practical upshot is that one size step costs 25 seconds for a soft egg and 45 for a hard one, so the table below reads across by doneness.

Extra-large eggs are the ones to watch at altitude, because the size and the height stack. At 5,000 feet an extra-large fridge egg needs 13 minutes 20 seconds to hard-boil, more than two minutes longer than at sea level. Check one egg before you cool the batch, and add a minute if the yolk is not set.

Room temperature saves the usual minute or so: an extra-large room-temperature egg needs 9 minutes 40 seconds to hard-boil, against 10 minutes 55 seconds from the fridge. For a soft egg the room-temperature time is 3 minutes 35 seconds, against 4 minutes 55 seconds from the fridge.

One shopping note: extra-large eggs are not always the same weight. USDA sizes are minimum weights per dozen, so individual eggs vary a little around 64 grams. A few grams either way moves the time by seconds. If your eggs feel unusually big for the carton, add 15 seconds and check one.
